notes.meaning: Ahaz was a wicked king of Judah. Two neighboring kings, Rezin of Aram (Syria) and Pekah of Israel, joined forces to attack Jerusalem. Isaiah tells us the ending first: they could not take the city. Its rescue came from God's kindness, not from human strength.

The "house of David" means King Ahaz and his court. "Ephraim" is another name for the northern kingdom of Israel, after its largest tribe. When they heard that the two kingdoms had joined against them, the king and the people shook like trees in a storm. Their fear grew out of guilt and weak faith. They had turned from God and did not know how to turn back.

God sent Isaiah to meet Ahaz even though Ahaz had not asked for him. Ahaz was probably out by the city's water supply, getting ready for a siege. Isaiah brought his son Shear-jashub, whose name means "a remnant will return." The boy's name itself was a message: the nation would not be wiped out completely.

God told Ahaz to calm down and not panic, and especially not to run for help from Assyria. The two kings looked like a raging fire. To God they were only the smoking ends of burnt-out sticks, nearly gone. Calling Pekah just "the son of Remaliah" was a put-down, because he had seized the throne by murder.

The two kings had a cruel plan: invade Judah, scare it into giving up, split it between themselves, and set up their own puppet king. Nobody knows who "the son of Tabeal" was. He was probably someone who opposed David's family. Their plan was really an attack on God's promise to keep David's line on the throne.
Against all their armies and schemes, God sets just His word: "It will not happen." People make plans, but God decides how things turn out. Whatever stands against God cannot stand for long.

Each enemy king would stay inside his own borders. Rezin would rule only Damascus, and he would not add Jerusalem to his kingdom. Isaiah also warns that within 65 years Israel (Ephraim) would be so broken it would no longer be a people. Many older commentators see this fulfilled when an Assyrian king named Esarhaddon carried off the last Israelites and moved foreigners into their land.

Pekah, too, would rule only Samaria and would not conquer Judah. Then comes the key line. In Hebrew it is a wordplay, something like "If you will not confide, you will not abide." Without trust in God, Ahaz and Judah would not stand. Faith is what quiets and steadies the heart in trouble.

Ahaz seems to have said nothing back. He was quietly trusting in Assyria instead. But God did not give up on him and spoke to him again through Isaiah. When God sees that a promise alone does not satisfy us, He kindly adds proof to help our weakness.

God offered Ahaz any sign he wanted, a miracle to prove the promise. He could choose anything from the depths of Sheol (the grave, the place of the dead) to the heights of heaven. God still called Himself "your God" to this wicked king, because Ahaz was a son of David. It was amazing patience toward someone who did not deserve it.

Ahaz's answer sounded holy. He quoted the rule against testing God (Deuteronomy 6:16). But it was a cover story. He had already decided to trust Assyria and did not want God to interfere. Accepting a sign that God Himself offers is not testing God; refusing it is a rebellion against Him.

Isaiah now speaks sharply to the whole royal family. They had already worn out the patience of God's messengers, the prophets. Now they were wearing out God's own patience too. Notice that Isaiah now says "my God." Ahaz would not claim God as his own, but Isaiah gladly does.

Even though Ahaz refused, God Himself would give a sign: a virgin would have a son and call Him Immanuel, which means "God with us." The traditional reading sees this fulfilled in Jesus, born of the virgin Mary (Matthew 1:23). Jesus is God come in a human body. How could this help Ahaz? The Messiah (God's promised King and Savior) had to come from David's family, so that family and nation could not be destroyed before He came.

differ.view: Many see a near and a far fulfilment. A child born in Isaiah's day was a sign that the two enemy kings would soon fall. Jesus, born of a virgin, is the full and final fulfilment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translators render it "this young woman is about to conceive." They say the Hebrew word does not by itself mean virgin. They think she was probably present at the scene, perhaps a member of the royal family.

notes.meaning: Curds and honey were ordinary food for little children in that land. This shows that the promised child would be truly human. He would be fed and grow up like other children until He was old enough to choose right from wrong. Some older commentators add that this simple food also hints at hard times, when the land would yield little else (see v. 22).

Within the few years it takes a small child to learn right from wrong, both enemy kings would be gone. Some think Isaiah meant his own son standing beside him. Others think he meant any young child. Either way, it came true: Assyria killed Rezin, and Pekah was murdered by Hoshea, who took his throne (2 Kings 16:9; 15:30).

The good news turns into a warning. God would bring the king of Assyria, the very king Ahaz trusted, against Judah. It would be the worst time since the ten northern tribes broke away from David's family. Isaiah saves the words "king of Assyria" for the very end, to make the warning hit hard.

God would only need to whistle, and the armies of Egypt (the "flies") and Assyria (the "bees") would come swarming. Both lands were known for those insects. They would settle everywhere: in valleys, rock caves and bushes. No hiding place would be safe. Even powerful nations are under God's control.

Ahaz had paid Assyria to help him (2 Kings 16:7-8). Now God would use that "hired razor" against Judah. Shaving the head, the body and even the beard pictures stripping the land bare, from the highest leaders to the lowest people. Cutting off a man's beard was a deep shame in that culture.

A man who once had large herds would feel lucky to keep one young cow and two sheep. Yet there would be plenty of milk. The fields would be empty for grazing, and very few people would be left to feed. The survivors would live on curds and wild honey, because no one would be farming.

Rich vineyards, worth a fortune, would turn into thorns and briers. People would go there with bows and arrows, to hunt wild animals or protect themselves from them. Hillsides once carefully farmed would become open pasture for cattle and sheep. Sin can turn a fruitful land into a wilderness.
